topic.subject: social
topic.title: Air and the atmosphere
topic.scope: composition of atmosphere, layers, weather and climate, temperature, air pressure, winds, moisture

nodes.name: Wind moves high to low pressure
Humidity is water vapor in air

misconceptions.statement: Oxygen is the most abundant gas because it is the most important for life.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse biological importance with physical quantity.
misconceptions.fix: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the air, while oxygen is only 21%.

probe.question: Which gas makes up the largest part of the air we breathe?

misconceptions.statement: Wind is caused by the air pushing itself forward.
misconceptions.why: Students struggle to visualize invisible pressure gradients.
misconceptions.fix: Wind is the horizontal movement of air from areas of high pressure to low pressure.

probe.question: Why does wind blow?
probe.wrong_answer: Air has a force that pushes it along.

misconceptions.statement: Humidity is the same as rain.
misconceptions.why: Students associate moisture only with visible liquid water.
misconceptions.fix: Humidity is the amount of invisible water vapor present in the air.

probe.question: Is the air humid if it is not raining?
probe.wrong_answer: No, humidity only happens when it rains.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: The atmosphere ends where the clouds end.
misconceptions.why: Students equate the visible extent of weather with the entire atmosphere.
misconceptions.fix: The atmosphere extends hundreds of kilometers above the surface, far beyond the clouds.

probe.question: Where does the atmosphere end?
probe.wrong_answer: At the top of the clouds.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Oxygen is the only gas that living things need from the air.
misconceptions.why: Lessons stress breathing oxygen, so students ignore other gases like carbon dioxide for plants and nitrogen for soil fertility.
misconceptions.fix: Plants use carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, and nitrogen is needed to make proteins (taken up via soil bacteria). Oxygen is only one of the useful gases.

probe.question: Which gas from air do green plants use to make food?
probe.wrong_answer: Oxygen, because it is the gas all living things need.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only oxygen matters among atmospheric gases

misconceptions.statement: Oxygen itself burns, like a fuel.
misconceptions.why: Students see fire grow in air and think oxygen is the thing being burnt.
misconceptions.fix: Oxygen supports burning; it is not a fuel. Fuel burns in the presence of oxygen.

probe.question: What happens to a candle in a closed jar of pure oxygen compared with fuel?
probe.wrong_answer: Oxygen is the thing that burns, so the oxygen is what is used as fuel.

misconceptions.statement: Air is made only of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.why: Students know breathing in oxygen and breathing out carbon dioxide, so they think these two make up the air.
misconceptions.fix: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases.

probe.question: Name the gases that make up air.

misconceptions.root_belief: Air equals the gases we breathe

misconceptions.statement: Air gets warmer as we go higher up in the troposphere because we get closer to the Sun.
misconceptions.why: Students think nearer to the Sun means hotter, ignoring that the ground heats the air.
misconceptions.fix: In the troposphere temperature falls with height, since the air is heated mainly from the warm Earth's surface.

probe.question: Is it warmer or colder at the top of a high mountain, and why?
probe.wrong_answer: Warmer, because the mountain top is closer to the Sun.

misconceptions.root_belief: Closer to the Sun always means hotter
misconceptions.source_hint: research on temperature and altitude conceptions

misconceptions.statement: Weather such as rain, clouds and storms happens in the stratosphere.
misconceptions.why: Students think all the upper sky is one region, or that planes and storms share the same height.
misconceptions.fix: Almost all weather happens in the troposphere, the lowest layer. The stratosphere is calm and holds the ozone layer.

probe.question: In which layer of the atmosphere do clouds and rain occur?

misconceptions.root_belief: Weather occurs in every atmospheric layer

misconceptions.statement: Air has no weight and therefore exerts no pressure.
misconceptions.why: Air is invisible and feels light, so students think it weighs nothing.
misconceptions.fix: Air has weight, and the air above us presses on every surface; this is air pressure, which we do not feel because it acts equally from all sides.

probe.question: Does the air around us press on our body?
probe.wrong_answer: No, air is weightless so it does not press on anything.

misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about air

misconceptions.statement: Wind blows from low pressure areas to high pressure areas.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the direction, thinking air is pulled into the crowded high-pressure zone.
misconceptions.fix: Wind blows from high pressure to low pressure areas, trying to even out the difference.

probe.question: A region has low pressure and its neighbour has high pressure. Which way does wind blow?
probe.wrong_answer: From the low-pressure area to the high-pressure area.

misconceptions.root_belief: Air moves toward the denser, higher pressure

misconceptions.statement: Hot air always holds less moisture because heat dries water out of it.
misconceptions.why: Students link heat with drying clothes and think hot air cannot carry water vapour.
misconceptions.fix: Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. Humidity is usually higher in hot, coastal places.

probe.question: Which can hold more water vapour: warm air or cold air?
probe.wrong_answer: Cold air, because heat dries the moisture out.
